analysis.one_liner: Requires safety testing and FDA approval of genetically engineered foods before they reach the market.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to committee and a subcommittee in March 2000 and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before Congress ended on January 3, 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have treated genetic constructs in food as "food additives" under federal law, meaning companies could not sell a genetically engineered food without first proving to the FDA that it is safe. Companies would have to hand over all their safety data — including data cutting against safety — most of which would be made public, and the FDA would have to specifically check for allergies, new toxins, and nutrition changes. It also imposed fees on petitioning companies to pay for the review and for safety research.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, especially the roughly 3-7% of Americans with food allergies, would gain a safety review before genetically engineered foods reach stores, plus public access to the safety data companies currently submit only voluntarily. Farmers and food companies marketing non-engineered products would benefit from clearer rules.

how_it_helps.text: It would close the gap under which genetically engineered foods reached supermarket shelves without mandatory pre-market safety testing, by amending the food additive rules of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act to cover them.
Companies would have to submit all safety data, including data that does not support a safety claim, and much of that data would be made available to the public for comment.
The FDA would have to specifically evaluate allergenicity, new toxins, and changes in nutrition, and could not approve a protein likely to be commonly or severely allergenic.
Manufacturers would have to notify the FDA of any later-learned adverse health effects, and violations could bring civil penalties of up to $100,000 each.

analysis.who_pays: Biotech and food companies, which would pay user fees for each petition, conduct extensive new allergen and toxicity testing, and face civil penalties of up to $100,000 per violation for selling unapproved genetically engineered foods. Some costs could trickle to consumers in food prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill would add mandatory pre-market testing, public disclosure of company safety data, and a possible ban on antibiotic-resistance markers, which seed and food companies argued would slow product development and raise costs that could be passed on to consumers.

The bill's premise — that genetic engineering is 'wholly different' from traditional breeding and requires new safety rules — was contested; the industry and the FDA of the time treated genetically engineered foods as substantially equivalent to conventional ones and saw existing review as adequate.

The user-fee structure ties the FDA's new review costs and research funding to petitions filed by the companies themselves, which gives the agency a reliance on the regulated industry's own applications.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — safety testing and public disclosure for genetically engineered foods before they reach the market — is real but hard to quantify, and the bill would slow approvals and raise compliance costs for seed and food companies, some of which could pass through to consumers. The allergen and disclosure provisions address the strongest documented risk of the technology. The main design weakness is that it relies on the FDA's petition process and industry fees rather than an independent testing program, which limits how much new scrutiny it actually adds.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Commerce Committee and its health subcommittee in March 2000, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Dennis Kucinich introduced the bill on March 9, 2000, with six original cosponsors including independents Bernie Sanders and Virgil Goode.
It attracted 12 cosponsors in total: 10 Democrats, 1 Republican, and 1 Independent.
It was referred to the House Committee on Commerce and then, on March 21, 2000, to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment.
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and it died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The biotech and food industries, which kept selling genetically engineered foods with no mandatory pre-market testing or public disclosure.

for.name: Rep. Dennis Kucinich
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sought mandatory pre-market safety testing for genetically engineered foods.

for.name: 12 cosponsors (10 Democrats, 1 Republican, 1 Independent)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Rep. Jack Metcalf (R-WA), Rep. John Conyers (D-MI), and independents Bernie Sanders and Virgil Goode.

against.name: Biotechnology and food industry
against.what_they_did: The agricultural biotechnology industry opposed mandatory pre-market safety testing and public disclosure of its data, favoring the voluntary FDA consultation process then in place. This influence does not appear in the congressional record.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan at the margins, with 12 cosponsors split 10 Democrats, 1 Republican, and 1 Independent, but it never got far enough for a recorded vote to show where the chambers stood.

industries.industry: Biotech seed and agricultural biotechnology companies
industries.note: The bill would subject every genetically engineered food to mandatory pre-market FDA approval, public disclosure of company safety data, allergen testing, and $100,000 civil penalties — ending the voluntary consultation system the industry operated under.

industries.industry: Food manufacturers using genetically engineered ingredients
industries.note: Because the definition covers food 'produced with' genetically engineered material, food processors would inherit the approval and notification obligations for ingredients already on shelves, facing re-approval within two years of the new rules.
